{{< include _workflow.qmd >}}

> This course teaches you to use playtest evidence to make better design decisions.
> You will plan a playtest, describe what happened, decide whether a change worked,
> and write it up as a finding your team can act on. It assumes **no statistics and
> no R**. It does assume you build games. Read this page first; it takes five
> minutes.

## What You Are Learning

You are not training to be a statistician. You are learning to answer four
questions about your own game, with evidence instead of opinion:

| Question | What you do | Where you learn it |
| :- | :- | :- |
| **What happened?** | Clean the data, describe it, look at it | Stage 1 |
| **Is the pattern credible?** | Compare builds or groups; relate one measure to another | Stages 2 and 3 |
| **What does it mean for the game?** | Interpret the result in terms of the player's experience | every stage |
| **What should we do next?** | Recommend a change, a fix, or the next test | every stage, written up in Stage 4 |

The strip at the top of every notes page is the same idea as a process. Start with
a question, decide what to measure, collect it, clean it, describe it, compare or
relate, interpret, act. The highlighted steps are the ones that page covers.

**Start with the question.** Every technique in these notes is here because it
answers a question a design team actually asks. If you cannot say what question a
number answers, you do not need the number yet ([rule 2](ten-rules.qmd)).

---

## The Four Stages

The course runs from October to March, alongside your group project.

| Stage | Question | When | What it gives you |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| **1 Foundations** | What happened? | October, one 3-hour class | Plan a playtest, read a dataset into R, describe it, plot it |
| **2 Comparing Evidence** | Did the change work? | October, one 3-hour class | Clean the raw data, compare two builds, judge whether the difference is real and whether it matters |
| **3 Relationships & Visual Evidence** | What else does the data tell us? | November to February, short clinics | Report-quality figures with `ggplot2`; how measures relate to each other, on your own project's data |
| **4 Evidence to Decision** | What should we do, and how do we report it? | March, one workshop | Combine your evidence into findings and recommendations, written up in Quarto |

Stages 1 and 2 use *Tidebreak*, a playtest dataset built for teaching. By Stage 3
your team will have its own playtest data, and the clinics work on that.

**For your project:** the final assessment report has the headings Executive
Summary, Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion, Conclusion, References and
Appendices. Everything in Stages 1–3 produces something that goes under one of them.
Stage 4 puts it together.

---

## The Route

Stages 1 and 2 are two 90-minute cycles each: a framing question, about 30 minutes
of theory from the notes, a 15-minute demo, then the lab. The notes hold more than
the theory slot covers. In class we cover each page's core; the rest is there for
when you need it.

| When | Notes | Lab | Demo |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |
| **Before Stage 1** | [R from First Principles](02-r-first-principles.qmd), with R open | [Lab 00](../labs/setting-up.qmd) | |
| **Stage 1, cycle 1** | [Planning a Playtest](01-planning-a-playtest.qmd), [Data, Variables and Types](03-data-and-types.qmd) | [Lab 01](../labs/reading-data.qmd) Part A | [Stage 1](../demos/stage-1.qmd) |
| **Stage 1, cycle 2** | [Describing Variables](04-describing-variables.qmd), [Distributions and Shape](05-distributions-and-shape.qmd) | [Lab 01](../labs/reading-data.qmd) Part B | [Stage 1](../demos/stage-1.qmd) |
| **Stage 2, cycle 1** | [Cleaning and Transforming](06-cleaning-and-transforming.qmd) | [Lab 02](../labs/comparing-builds.qmd) Part A | [Stage 2](../demos/stage-2.qmd) |
| **Stage 2, cycle 2** | [From Sample to Population](07-sample-to-population.qmd), [Comparing Groups](08-comparing-groups.qmd) | [Lab 02](../labs/comparing-builds.qmd) Part B | [Stage 2](../demos/stage-2.qmd) |
| **Stage 3 clinics** | [Visualising with ggplot2](09-visualising-with-ggplot2.qmd), [Relationships and Correlation](10-relationships-and-correlation.qmd) | [Lab 03](../labs/clinic-figures.qmd), [Lab 04](../labs/clinic-relationships.qmd) | [Stage 3](../demos/stage-3.qmd) |
| **Stage 4 workshop** | [Interpreting and Reporting Evidence](11-reporting-evidence.qmd), [Combining Evidence](12-combining-evidence.qmd) | [Lab 05](../labs/complete-analysis.qmd) | [Stage 4](../demos/stage-4.qmd) |

**The R you will write.** You handle data with the tidyverse: `read_csv()` to load
it, then `filter()`, `select()`, `group_by()` and `summarise()` joined with the pipe,
`|>`. In Stages 1 and 2 you plot with base R (`hist()`, `boxplot()`, `plot()`),
which is quick and good for looking at data while you think. Stage 3 introduces
`ggplot2`, for figures other people will read. There is one way to do each job.
Where you will meet other ways in code you find online, the notes say so, and you
only need to recognise them.

## How a Notes Page Works

Every notes page has the same shape, so you always know where to look.

| Part | What it is for |
| :- | :- |
| **Opening quote** | What the page is for, and the playtest question running through it |
| **At a glance** | The stage, the time it takes, what to read first, key terms, the R you will write |
| **Why This Matters** | Why a games team needs the idea at all |
| **Core sections** | One idea each: what it is and why you need it, a figure, the *Tidebreak* example, the R, how you would say it in a report, and the common mistake |
| **Worked Example** | The page's question answered step by step, often overturning the obvious answer |
| **Interpretation Guidance** | What the data shows, what it suggests, and what you can legitimately conclude |
| **Common Mistakes** | The errors that turn up in real reports |
| **Practice** | A few short questions, with the answers in one collapsed box underneath |
| **Summary and Key Terms** | The page in a few lines, and a glossary for revision |

**Not everything is core.** Sections are marked when they are not:

- No label: **core**. You need to understand this and be able to use it.
- **Useful when needed**: depends on your game and your data. Read it when your
  project needs it.
- **Going further**: depth and background. Interesting, sometimes useful, never
  required. Collapsed boxes titled "Going further" and "The maths, if you want it"
  are the same.

**Every number is computed.** Each number in the prose is calculated from the data
when the page is built, so it cannot be out of date or mistyped. Figures stamped
*Illustration* use simulated data to show an idea cleanly; everything else is
*Tidebreak*.

**Type the code.** Every chunk runs as shown, provided the data sits in the `data/`
folder of your project. Typing it, rather than copying it, is how it sticks.

---

## The Labs and Reference Pages

**The labs** are where you do the analysis. Each exercise is tagged by what it asks
of you:

| Tier | What it asks | Time |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `[Do]` | One function, one result | 2–3 minutes |
| `[Apply]` | Combine two or three ideas | 5 minutes |
| `[Decide]` | A judgement call with no single right answer | 5–8 minutes |

Every exercise ends by asking you to write a sentence or two about what the result
means. That is the part that matters. Anyone can run a t-test; the course is about
knowing what the result means for the game. Solutions are collapsed under each
exercise. Open them after you have tried, even when your attempt worked.

**The reference pages** are for looking things up during a lab or in your project:

- [Statistics Reference](../reference/reference-statistics.qmd): every term in plain
  English, with an example and the common mistake
- [R and Quarto Reference](../reference/r-quarto-reference.qmd): every function, by
  task
- [ggplot2 Reference](../reference/reference-ggplot2.qmd): the figures you need from
  Stage 3

**The [Ten Rules](ten-rules.qmd)** are ten things to check every time you read
playtest data. Pages and labs point to them by number: "rule 5 again" means that
page.

---

## The Game: *Tidebreak*

*Tidebreak* is a fictional four-player top-down arena game. Two builds were
playtested: Build B added signposting to help players find their way. The playtest
produced the files every page uses:

| File | One row is | Used for |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `tidebreak_sessions.csv` | one player in one session | almost everything |
| `tidebreak_sessions_raw.csv` | the same, as exported, with faults | cleaning |
| `tidebreak_survey.csv` | one post-session survey | ratings and reporting |
| `tidebreak_paired.csv` | one player who played both builds | the paired comparison |
| `tidebreak_frame_times.csv` | one rendered frame | performance |

The data is synthetic, but it was built so that a careful analysis finds real
findings, and several of them contradict the obvious first answer. **That is the
point.** If a result surprises you, you are probably reading the data correctly.

## Before Stage 1

1. Work through [Lab 00: Setting Up](../labs/setting-up.qmd), and check that the
   test document renders.
2. Read [R from First Principles](02-r-first-principles.qmd) with R open beside you.
3. Skim the [Ten Rules](ten-rules.qmd). You will meet each of them properly later.

Then start with [Planning a Playtest](01-planning-a-playtest.qmd).
